body:
_Migrated from issue #1151, filed 2026-07-26._

Found while reviewing #1149 (cross-family review, proofed). Low severity, but the code no longer does what its docstring says.

## What

`CalibreDB.refresh_for_new_data()` iterates `CalibreDB.instances` and calls `expire_all()` / `rollback()` on `inst.session`. Since #1149, `session` is a property that resolves through the `scoped_session` registry, so `inst.session` returns **the session of whichever greenlet is executing the loop** — the same object on every iteration, regardless of how many instances there are. Sessions belonging to other in-flight requests are not reached.

The docstring's "on every CalibreDB instance" is therefore inaccurate: it refreshes one session N times.

## Why it is low severity

- The only caller is the manual reconnect endpoint (`cps/cwa_functions.py:684`).
- Sessions live exactly one request — `shutdown_session` removes the greenlet's session on every teardown — so every request that *starts* after the refresh gets a new session and sees the new data.
- The staleness window is only the tail of requests already in flight when the endpoint runs.

So the user-visible effect is close to nil today, and it self-heals. It is filed rather than fixed because the loop's intent genuinely is not achieved, and a future caller (a background refresh, say) would be misled by it.

## Direction

Iterating `CalibreDB.instances` cannot fix this — instances are not what owns a session. It needs either an operation that enumerates live registry entries and expires each, or a generation/invalidation counter that a session checks lazily on next use. The second is likely simpler and avoids touching other greenlets' sessions from outside, which is what #1150 was about.

Related: #1121, #1150.
title: refresh_for_new_data() only refreshes the calling request's session, not other in-flight ones
